items.title: Meer grip op je content: 5 tips voor meer overzicht en minder stress
items.raw_text: Hoe houd je als contentmarketeer grip op je tijd, strategie en planning? Tijdens een workshopdag wisselden MarCom-medewerkers van bibliotheken praktische tips en ervaringen uit. Ontdek de belangrijkste inzichten. Als contentmarketeer ben je naast creëren, bezig met managen. Hoe richt je je eigen tijd efficiënt in, bewaak je de contentstrategie en geef je gehoor aan je collega’s – zonder de grip op de te maken en publiceren content te verliezen? Een groep MarCom-medewerkers uit bibliotheken kwam begin oktober 2026 samen, omringd door de groene omgeving van De Tuin van de Smid in Leiden, om antwoord te vinden op die vraag. Tijdens een inspirerende workshopdag onder leiding van Jessie de Booij en Probiblio wisselden zij ervaringen, uitdagingen en praktische oplossingen uit. De belangrijkste inzichten zetten we voor je op een rij. 1. Leg focus aan met contentpijlers Veel contentproblemen beginnen met een gebrek aan focus. Maar, als alles belangrijk is, wordt het lastig om keuzes te maken. Contentpijlers helpen daarbij. Door vooraf te bepalen welke thema’s centraal staan, ontstaat er richting en samenhang. Dit maakt het eenvoudiger om nieuwe ideeën en verzoeken te toetsen: past dit binnen onze strategie of niet? items.title: Ledenonderzoek 2025: bibliotheken scoren goed op gastvrijheid en maatschappelijke waarde
items.raw_text: Bibliotheekleden zijn enthousiast over hun bibliotheek. Ze waarderen vooral de gastvrije medewerkers, fijne sfeer en maatschappelijke waarde. Toch zien ze ook ruimte voor verbetering, bijvoorbeeld bij werk- en studieplekken en de inrichting. Wat kunnen bibliotheken leren van deze inzichten uit het BiebPanel Ledenonderzoek? Wat is het BiebPanel Ledenonderzoek 2025? Het instrument BiebPanel bestaat uit diverse onderzoeken, waaronder het lokale ledenonderzoek. Het ledenonderzoek bestaat uit verschillende modules, die elk een specifiek thema uitdiepen (bijv. Lidmaatschap of Collectie). Hieronder beschrijven we enkele interessante inzichten uit het ledenonderzoek van 2025. Leden zijn over het algemeen enthousiast over hun bibliotheek en bevelen deze sterk aan. Hierdoor krijgt de bibliotheek een hoge NPS (aanbevelingsscore), met name onder jongere leden en 75-plussers. Wel zijn er lokaal – zowel tussen bibliotheekorganisaties als tussen vestigingen – grote verschillen in de NPS. Werk- en studieplekken en horeca- of warme drankvoorziening worden minder positief beoordeeld. De helft van de leden vindt de bibliotheek goed zoals deze nu is. items.title: Inwonersonderzoek: Ook wie de bibliotheek niet bezoekt, ziet haar waarde
items.raw_text: Ook wie de bibliotheek niet bezoekt, ziet de waarde ervan. Dat blijkt uit het Probiblio BiebPanel Inwonersonderzoek onder ruim 1.600 niet-gebruikers. De meeste inwoners vinden de bibliotheek belangrijk voor de samenleving, maar weten lang niet altijd wat er allemaal te doen is. Wat betekent dit voor bibliotheken en waar liggen kansen? Wat is het BiebPanel Inwonersonderzoek? Het instrument BiebPanel bestaat uit verschillende onderzoeken, waaronder het tweejaarlijkse, inwonersonderzoek. Hieronder worden een aantal interessante uitkomsten van het landelijke inwonersonderzoek 2026 uitgelicht. Dat de bibliotheek ook betekenis heeft voor mensen die er zelf geen gebruik van maken, blijkt uit het BiebPanel Inwonersonderzoek. Het onderzoek vond plaats in het voorjaar van 2026, onder een representatieve steekproef van ruim 1600 inwoners van Nederland die geen lid of bezoeker zijn van de bibliotheek. De ruime meerderheid van inwoners vindt de bibliotheek belangrijk voor de samenleving, ook al komen zij er zelf niet. Vooral 75-plussers zien het belang van de bibliotheek, maar ook de meeste inwoners onder de 36 jaar vinden dat de bibliotheek mensen helpt om nieuwe dingen te leren en/of belangrijk is voor de samenleving. Daarnaast geldt: hoe hoger inwoners zijn opgeleid, hoe vaker zij de waarde van de bibliotheek erkennen. items.title: Burgerschap in het onderwijs

items.title: “Met het relevantiekader voerde ik het juiste gesprek met de gemeente”
items.raw_text: Stel: je bent een kersverse bibliotheekdirecteur en de gemeente stelt een werkwijze voor die vragen oproept over de gelijkwaardige rolve rdeling tussen bibliotheek en gemeente . Martje van Nes van Bibliotheek Schiedam koos ervoor het gesprek met de gemeente aan te gaan. Met hulp van Probiblio en het relevantiekader wist ze het gesprek te kantelen van producten en prestaties naar maatschappelijke waarde. In 2024 trad Martje van Nes aan als directeur van Bibliotheek Schiedam. Het was direct een uitdagende periode voor de subsidie van de bibliotheek. Hoe was de relatie met de gemeente bij jouw aantreden? “Het meerjarenbeleid van de bibliotheek én de termijn van het College kwamen tegelijk ten einde. Het was bekend dat er bezuinigd moesten worden maar het was nog onduidelijk wat de bezuinigingen precies voor de bibliotheek zouden betekenen. Ik had nog geen ervaring in het werken met gemeentelijke procedures, maar met die kennis is het achterhoofd was ik wel extra alert in het contact richting de gemeente, onze subsidieverstrekker.” In het gesprek met de gemeente stelde de ambtenaar voor met een producten- & dienstencatalogus te gaan werken. Ik vond het een goed idee om inzichtelijk te maken wat de bibliotheek bijdraagt aan de stad Schiedam. De vorm van een producten- en dienstencatalogus past mijns inziens echter niet bij hoe de rolverdeling van gemeente en bibliotheek eruit ziet op basis van de publieke waarden. items.title: Handreiking Maatschappelijk verantwoord ondernemen: maak de impact van jouw bibliotheek zichtbaar
items.raw_text: Bibliotheken maken iedere dag maatschappelijk verschil. Van het bevorderen van kansengelijkheid en digitale inclusie tot het creëren van ontmoetingsplekken en het verduurzamen van de organisatie. Maar hoe zorg je ervoor dat maatschappelijk verantwoord ondernemen (MVO) niet alleen iets is wat je doet, maar ook een vast onderdeel wordt van je strategie? Deze handreiking helpt jou om MVO concreet en meetbaar te maken. items.title: Is jouw bibliotheek goed verzekerd? Dat weet je pas als je het controleert
items.raw_text: Zijn bibliotheken eigenlijk wel goed verzekerd? Die vraag leeft binnen de sector. Bij Bibliotheek AanZet bleek na een kritische doorlichting dat er verbeteringen mogelijk waren. In dit interview vertelt Marloes Duijvestijn van FACO Advies na een uitgebreid traject bij AanZet waar bibliotheken op moeten letten en welke lessen uit de praktijk te trekken zijn. VOB Handreiking Verzekeren binnen Governance, Risk & Compliance De VOB publiceert met enige regelmaat een actuele versie van de Handreiking Governance, Risk & Compliance (GRC), bedoeld om bibliotheken te helpen met het gestructureerd en geïntegreerd aanpakken van deze onderling verbonden aspecten van maatschappelijk verantwoord ondernemen. De Handreiking Verzekeren van de VOB (binnenkort beschikbaar) sluit op die publicatie aan. Verzekeren is namelijk een manier om risico’s te managen die weliswaar niet vaak voorkomen maar áls ze voorkomen grote (financiële) impact hebben. Een organisatie die adequaat verzekerd is – niet on(der)verzekerd, niet oververzekerd en niet meer premie betalen dan nodig – doet aan goed risicomanagement (risk) en wordt daarmee op dit onderdeel goed bestuurd (governance). Sommige risico’s doen zich maar zelden voor, maar kunnen áls het misgaat grote gevolgen hebben. Juist dan is het belangrijk dat een verzekering goed aansluit op wat een bibliotheek nodig heeft. items.title: Terugblik studiereis Letland

items.title: Persoonlijke aandacht als basis voor goede onboarding bij KopGroep Bibliotheken
items.raw_text: Een bloemetje op de eerste werkdag, kennismaken met collega’s en vooral regelmatig vragen: hoe gaat het met je? Bij KopGroep Bibliotheken draait onboarding om persoonlijke aandacht en verbinding. Desiree van Ham, HR-manager bij KopGroep Bibliotheken, vertelt hoe zij nieuwe medewerkers begeleiden, waarom zij de organisatie als een ‘warm bad’ ervaren en hoe waardevol de samenwerking binnen het bibliotheeknetwerk daarbij is. items.title: De kracht van leesclubs
items.raw_text: Aan een grote tafel in de bibliotheek zitten acht mensen gezellig bij elkaar. Een kop thee binnen handbereik, acht dezelfde boeken op tafel. Ze praten over het verhaal dat ze allemaal hebben gelezen. Wat raakte hen? Welke personages bleven hangen? En was het einde nu briljant of juist verwarrend? Welkom bij de leesclub. Een boek samen lezen verbindt. In dit artikel lees je hoe Rijnbrink leesclubs ondersteunt, wat de meerwaarde is voor bibliotheken en welke kansen er liggen voor de toekomst. Meer dan samen lezen Met anderen praten over boeken verbreedt je blik op de wereld. Daarnaast stimuleren leesclubs het lezen van nieuwe boeken en zorgen ze voor ontmoeting. Niet online, maar juist fysiek. In de bibliotheek, bijvoorbeeld, of bij een van de deelnemers thuis. Juist daarom zijn leesclubs een waardevolle aanvulling op het aanbod van bibliotheken. Een leesclub bestaat meestal uit vijf tot tien mensen die hetzelfde boek lezen en daar samen over in gesprek gaan. Maar hoe zorg je ervoor dat al die lezers hetzelfde boek kunnen lenen? Daarom ondersteunt Rijnbrink leesclubs via MijnLeesclub.nl, een centraal platform voor leesclubs in Overijssel, Flevoland, Noord-Holland en Zuid-Holland. En binnenkort ook in Gelderland. items.title: Visietraject bij MFCO Rozet: de kunst van impactgericht werken
items.raw_text: Ga je een verandertraject altijd in omdat iets niet goed gaat? Nee, blijkt uit het verhaal van Rozet. Bij deze Arnhemse multifunctionele culturele organisatie (MFCO) zaten de adviseurs Taal en Cultuur behoorlijk op een lijn. De samenwerking binnen team Educatie verliep organisch en intuïtief. items.title: Schuren mag! 7x inzichten over democratie en burgerschap
items.raw_text: Een literaire avond in je bibliotheek over een onderwerp dat gevoelig ligt. Een school die een collectie afwijst vanwege levensovertuigingen. items.title: AI-vermeldingen, CAPTCHA en meer: praktische tips voor privacy en informatiebeveiliging

items.title: Maak kennis met Constance: de kracht achter de onderwijscollecties
items.raw_text: Tussen de boekenkasten in het collectiegebouw van Rijnbrink werkt Constance Melissen. Als collectiebeheerder Onderwijs zorgt zij ervoor dat scholen boeken krijgen die aansluiten bij hun lessen én de leefwereld van kinderen en jongeren. Zo draagt ze bij aan leesplezier bij de jeugd. In dit artikel maak je kennis met Constance en het werk dat zij doet. Wie regelmatig op een basisschool komt, herkent het meteen: de themahoek. Vaak vol met boeken in een bepaald thema. Soms door de leerkracht aangevuld met accessoires. Een thema is bijvoorbeeld kerst, of vervoer. Maar ook duurzaamheid of sprookjes. Bij Rijnbrink noemen we dit onderwijscollecties. De boeken zijn verzameld rondom een thema. Ze sluiten aan bij de leefwereld van kinderen en passen bij het niveau van verschillende leeftijdsgroepen in het basisonderwijs en de kinderopvang. Zo ontdekken kinderen nieuwe onderwerpen en lezen ze boeken die aansluiten bij hun interesses en ontwikkeling. Ook helpt het de leraren bij het geven van hun lessen. Scholen kunnen zelf online een themacollectie bestellen en deze zes weken lenen. Werken tussen de boeken Constance is verantwoordelijk voor de onderwijscollecties. Zij bepaalt welke boeken bij een thema passen. En zorgt ervoor dat het pakket met themaboeken bij de scholen komen. Haar werk doet ze letterlijk tussen de boeken. items.title: Frisse financiële start in 2027? 5x tips voor jouw jaarafsluiting
items.raw_text: Het jaar loopt op zijn einde. Een mooi moment om even stil te staan, terug te kijken en vooruit te denken. Wat ging er goed, wat kan beter? Wat moet er financieel nog geregeld worden? items.title: Op weg naar slimmer en duurzamer transport
items.raw_text: We merken het allemaal aan de pomp: de prijs van brandstof is hoog. Maandelijks betaalt Rijnbrink nu €3.000 meer aan brandstof dan een jaar geleden. Het is daarom noodzakelijk om efficiënt en duurzaam te rijden. Misschien merk je dat als bibliotheek of school, omdat we materialen op een andere tijd bezorgen dan je gewend bent. In dit artikel vertellen collega’s Hans Bender en Daan Meijer van Facilitair & Logistiek over hoe zij werken aan efficiënt en toekomstbestendig transport. Waar willen zij naartoe? Welke uitdagingen zijn er? En wat betekent dit voor jullie? Hans en Daan kijken vanaf hun werkruimte uit op het wagenpark van Rijnbrink. Vanuit de distributiehal vertrekken dagelijks bestel- en vrachtauto’s naar scholen en bibliotheken in Gelderland en Overijssel. Wekelijks bezoeken onze chauffeurs zo’n 210 vestigingen en maken zij ongeveer 650 stops. Niet alle voertuigen gaan iedere dag de weg op. Hans: ‘Van de elf wagens die eerst dagelijks reden, rijden er nu nog maar negen. items.title: Groeien in je rol als vrijwilligerscoördinator, hoe doe je dat?

items.title: Prinsjesdag 2026: 5 thema’s uitgelicht voor bibliotheken
items.raw_text: Prinsjesdag 2026 zit erop. De nieuw gepresenteerde plannen laten zien dat het kabinet vertrouwen heeft in de toekomst van bibliotheken. Er komt meer zekerheid voor leesbevordering, bibliotheken krijgen een belangrijke maatschappelijke rol en er is geld voor verdere ontwikkeling. Tegelijkertijd zijn er ook uitdagingen. Structureel geld voor leesbevordering Goed nieuws is dat de programma’s BoekStart en de Bibliotheek op school vanaf 2027 structurele financiering krijgen. items.title: Nederlanders denken dat ze phishing herkennen, maar AI maakt oplichting steeds echter en juist dát is een groot veiligheidsrisico
items.raw_text: Uit het jaarlijkse nationale cybersecurityonderzoek van Alert Online, mede mogelijk gemaakt door het ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, blijkt dat Nederlanders wél weten wat veilig online gedrag is, maar gemiddeld slechts een derde van de veilige handelingen consequent toepassen. Den Haag – Nederlanders weten goed hoe ze zich online moeten beschermen, maar vertrouwen opvallend vaak op hun eigen vermogen om gevaar te herkennen. Zodra er meer van hen gevraagd wordt dan kijken, neemt de motivatie om zich veilig te gedragen af. Slechts één op de zes gebruikt altijd tweefactorauthenticatie, een dubbel slot voor je accounts en apparaten dat ervoor zorgt dat er meer nodig is dan een wachtwoord om in te loggen. items.title: Podcastaflevering over Digitaal Doordacht en de praktijkimpact van digitalisering
items.raw_text: ECP-directeur Arie van Bellen ging in een recente aflevering van de podcastreeks ECP Talks in gesprek met ECP-programmaregisseur Sabine Herbrink over het programma Digitaal Doordacht. Zij bespraken hoe het programma de overheid helpt om bewuste, doordachte keuzes te maken in onze snel digitaliserende samenleving. Het gesprek ging niet alleen over de kansen zoals dwarsverbanden tussen thema’s en de meerwaarde die het programma biedt in de digitalisering van de overheid, maar ook over de uitdagingen rondom verantwoorde inzet, innovatie en samenwerking. items.title: Van regisserende naar ontwerpende overheid

Zo laten de verhalen zien hoe digitalisering door concrete interventies kan bijdragen aan een toekomstgerichte overheid waarin burgers en ondernemers centraal staan, met blijvende aandacht voor ethiek, privacy, security en maatschappelijk vertrouwen. Op 24 juni vond in Amare voor de vijfde keer de CIO-dag plaats. Hun verhaal begint bij taalmodellen, maar raakt al snel aan een veel fundamentelere vraag: hoe houdt de overheid zelf regie over haar digitale toekomst? Binnen de Nederlandse Digitaliseringsstrategie is AI daarom een prioriteit: de overheid wil AI verantwoord inzetten voor maatschappelijke opgaven en betere dienstverlening, succesvolle toepassin

items.title: OTC Whitepaper Soevereiniteit
items.raw_text: Digitale soevereiniteit betekent niet dat organisaties alle digitale diensten zelf moeten bezitten of beheren. Het betekent dat zij aantoonbare grip hebben op kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden: inzicht in de keten, bewuste risicoacceptatie, uitvoerbare alternatieven, onafhankelijke controle en transparante communicatie over keuzes en restrisico’s. In het whitepaper over digitale soevereiniteit vertaalt de Online Trust Coalitie dit thema naar een praktisch handelingskader voor bestuurders, IT-verantwoordelijken, toezichthouders, serviceproviders en risk- en compliancefuncties. De OTC stelt dat digitale soevereiniteit niet draait om volledige autonomie of autarkie, maar om aantoonbare beheersing: inzicht in kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden, expliciete risicoafweging, uitvoerbare exit-mogelijkheden, onafhankelijke controle en heldere communicatie over restrisico’s en gemaakte keuzes. De OTC signaleert dat impliciet vertrouwen in digitale diensten onder druk staat. items.title: ‘Veranderen doe je via consensus én met fermheid’
items.raw_text: Binnen Digitaal Doordacht onderzoeken we hoe digitalisering in de publieke sector daadwerkelijk bijdraagt aan betere dienstverlening, meer openheid en groter vertrouwen. Het veranderverhaal van Jolein Baidenmann laat zien dat echte openheid niet draait om simpelweg méér informatie openbaar maken, maar om informatie die voor mensen daadwerkelijk begrijpelijk en bruikbaar is. Wat haar aanpak bijzonder maakt, is hoe zij in een complexe publieke omgeving beweging creëert: door belangen zichtbaar te maken, partijen te verbinden en draagvlak te combineren met duidelijke keuzes. “Soms moet je als leider keuzes maken en stevig zijn: ik heb iedereen gehoord, maar we gaan toch die kant op.” Jolein Baidenmann is verandermanager en werkt met die insteek aan een overheid die openheid op een betekenisvolle manier probeert waar te maken. “Het is belangrijk dat een open overheid de samenleving in staat stelt om mee te denken, te controleren en gebruik te maken van de informatie die bij de overheid beschikbaar is.” Als manager Open Overheid en plaatsvervangend directeur Open Overheid bij het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) is Baidenmann bij uitstek de persoon om het concept ‘open overheid’ in praktijk te brengen. items.raw_text: Wednesday, November 4 | 16:00 – 17:30 CET Register to Attend Abstract Libraries are increasingly data-driven, but when it comes to digital collections, we still face a basic challenge: before we can measure consistently, we need to agree on what we are measuring. The “digital library” or “digital collection” can mean very different things to different institutions and professionals. Rather than aiming for a single standardized definition, today’s webinar is an opportunity to share perspectives, experiences, and approaches to collecting data about digital collections and their users. Our focus is on learning from one another and exploring the different ways we understand and work with these collections. We hope today’s discussion will help move the conversation forward. items.title: MetLib 2026 | Day 3: Rethinking Public Spaces and the Future of Librarianship
items.raw_text: Can the internet become a genuine public space rather than a collection of platforms dominated by commercial interests? This question opened the third day of MetLib 2026 , as keynote speaker Jantien Borsboom explored alternative models of digital public spaces and the role libraries could play in creating online environments that serve people rather than profit. The impact of artificial intelligence and the future of shared knowledge were also central themes. Erin Kissane addressed the challenges of maintaining public trust and collective understanding in an increasingly fragmented digital world. The day concluded with David Lankes , who invited participants to imagine librarianship in 2036, asking: Will librarians still focus primarily on collections and materials, or will they become community practitioners? His keynote challenged traditional definitions of the profession and highlighted the importance of flexibility of it. Throughout the day, discussions offered new perspectives on libraries — not merely as third places or community hubs, but as essential civic infrastructure , supporting democratic participation and social connections. Another intriguing idea was to see libraries as fitness centres for the mind , where people can exercise curiosity, creativity and critical thinking, just as they exercise their bodies in gyms. items.title: MetLib 2026 | Day 2: Be Bold – Rethinking the Library of the Future
items.raw_text: The second day of the Metlib Conference 2026 challenged library professionals from around the world to be bold, rethink traditional approaches and explore innovative models that are reshaping the role of public libraries. Hosted by Amsterdam Public Library (OBA), the day brought together inspiring keynote speakers and practical examples of how libraries can respond creatively to a rapidly changing world. Loes Damhof opened the discussions by exploring the importance of public spaces in an increasingly accelerated society. She invited participants to imagine libraries as places where people can slow down, reflect and explore possibilities — spaces that create room for what lies between the present and the future. Martin Berendse introduced OBA Next, an ambitious project that approaches the library of the future not as a finished building, but as an evolving concept. Its temporary laboratory, opened in 2025 in partnership with TUMO, is already experimenting with new ways of learning, creating and engaging young people, ahead of the planned permanent library in 2030. Building on this theme, Pegor Papazian, co-founder of TUMO, presented a different vision of education, drawing on his experience of working with teenagers and young adults. His approach emphasised independent exploration, creativity and learning by doing, encouraging young people to take ownership of their learning. items.title: Information Integrity in the Age of AI: Brazil’s Approach to Trustworthy Government Publications
items.raw_text: By Carla Maria Martellote Viola, Senior Researcher, Brazilian Institute of Information in Science and Technology (Ibict), Brazil As governments increasingly use Artificial Intelligence (AI) to draft, organize and deliver information, a central question is becoming unavoidable: how can the integrity of government publications be protected when generative AI is part of the information-production process? In Brazil, this issue is gaining relevance alongside the Brazilian Artificial Intelligence Plan (PBIA 2024–2028), “AI for the Good of All”, which combines technological development with social inclusion, protection of rights, information integrity and responsible AI governance [1]. Information integrity involves more than factual correctness. It depends on information being accurate, complete, reliable and sufficiently contextualized, while its origin and transformations remain traceable. In institutional environments, these attributes support transparency and public trust and help reduce the risks of error, manipulation and bias. Provenance is especially important because it allows the origin, trajectory and modifications of information to be identified and its authenticity to be assessed [2]. For government publications, where citizens may rely on official information to understand rights, policies and public services, these requirements acquire particular significance. items.title: From Beirut to Byblos: LAU Libraries as a Beacon of Hope
items.raw_text: By Caline Trad , IFLA-GIOPS -Information Coordinator and Dr. Jordan Srour , Interim Dean of Libraries and Information Resources, LAU Running three academic libraries across two campuses is not easy in normal times. The Lebanese American University Libraries are at the heart of our campuses; they are the space where students go to study, to meet, to learn, to explore, to create, to print or to just relax. With so much activity anything can and does happen on an average day…now add a war. LAU’s response to the renewal of Israeli hostilities on 2 March 2026, followed standard protocols: a rapid move to online learning . While moving learning online sounds easy it belies a reality of stress and anxiety with students afraid that their grades will be impacted because their bandwidth falters. Against this backdrop, the LAU Libraries made a commitment to remain open to ensure that all learners could come to campus to access stable internet and electricity. Again, not an easy decision. Opening the libraries meant requiring staff to be present on campus – even in the face of streets that were crowded with displaced Lebanese, fuel prices that multiplied, and drones that circled – and still circle – overhead. War altered the meaning of librarianship inside the three LAU libraries. Unique in the design of the Riyad Nassar Library (RNL) in Beirut, is the fact that it doubles as an airstrike shelter. items.title: Authors Discuss Being Banned, Part 2: Malinda Lo, Ellen Hopkins, and Jennifer L. Armentrout
items.raw_text: The troubling trend of book challenges and bans in libraries across the US continues. In 2025, 4,235 titles were banned or challenged at public, school, or university libraries, according to the American Library Association’s (ALA) State of America’s Libraries 2026 report. This figure was the second highest (following the record set in 2023) since ALA’s Office for Intellectual Freedom (OIF) began documenting censorship attempts in 1990. Behind each title is an author being professionally—and sometimes personally—targeted for the stories they have chosen to share. These works usually amplify marginalized voices such as abuse victims or those within the LGBTQ+ community. American Libraries spoke with five authors on the Top 11 Most Challenged Books of 2025 list included in the report to hear how their experiences affected them. Interviews have been edited for space and clarity. Read Part 1 for the first two interviews with Patricia McCormick and Stephen Chbosky. Set in 1950s San Francisco, the book tells the story of 17-year-old Lily Hu as she navigates falling in love in a place and time not ready to accept a same-sex couple. items.title: Refreshing for the Future
items.raw_text: Library renovations can feel overwhelming—especially when you’re juggling tight budgets, big community expectations, and a building that’s showing its age. The good news is you don’t have to choose between “do nothing” and “tear it down.” Most successful library upgrades live somewhere in the middle: a smart, phased plan that protects your long-term vision while making meaningful improvements right now. Here are a few practical ways to think about approaching a library renovation: Start with a North Star. Before you pick finishes or start talking timelines, take a step back and get clarity on what you want your library to become. I call this the north star —your vision for how the building should function for staff and the public. Even if you only have funding for part of the work today, guiding principles help you avoid spending money on changes you’ll undo later. Renovations are much easier when everyone can point to the same end goal—even if you’re getting there in phases. Assess the building first. It’s tempting to jump straight into visible improvements, but understanding existing conditions is what sets a project up for success. A solid facility-condition evaluation looks at the status of major building systems and flags components that may be nearing the end of their life cycle, such as mechanical systems, electrical panel capacity, and even finishes like carpet. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. items.title: 2026 Library Design Showcase
items.raw_text: Welcome to American Libraries’ 2026 Library Design Showcase, our annual celebration of new and renovated libraries across the US and Canada. The word welcome appeared in many of this year’s submissions, reflecting a growing understanding that in anxious times, the library is a place that should feel good: safe, comfortable, well-lit, plugged in, and deeply connected to its surroundings. More than two-thirds of this year’s 15 selections are renovations or adaptive reuse projects. Libraries of all types are finding ways to acknowledge historical and environmental realities, embrace natural elements and cultural identities, evolve traditions, and build in flexibility to account for the unexpected. Read on for snapshots of these communities in motion. Natural immersion Maplewood (N.J.) Memorial Library Adjacent to a historic park, with protected natural areas on all sides, this 1955 masonry structure had nowhere to expand but up. The new, light-filled second floor features bird-safe glass, wood battens, and green roofs for a treehouse feel. The all-electric building, the first LEED Gold–certified library in New Jersey, includes solar panels that offset more than half of the library’s energy use. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . And as more schools across the country enact phone-free policies—29 states and the District of Columbia have instituted bell-to-bell phone-free policies so far—many school libraries are experiencing a surge in popularity. items.title: Open Movements: Recognizing Challenges and Building Connections (New Book From ACRL)
items.raw_text: Note: The book is available for purchase in print . An open access edition is also available. From ALA: The Association of College and Research Libraries (ACRL) announces the publication of “ Open Movements: Recognizing Challenges and Building Connections ,” edited by Abbey K. Elder, Shannon M. Smith, and Bryan Ricupero. This collection surfaces the work taking place across open movements and highlights how practitioners and advocates can effectively collaborate for sustainable change. Open movements all center public access and broad representation, and work to prevent the concentration of power governing information and its monetization. As general discussion of openness has narrowed to focus on areas like open science, data, access, and education, these individual communities have grown distanced from each other and, occasionally, their shared values. In five sections, “Open Movements: Recognizing Challenges and Building Connections” explores different perspectives on open and how the values that guide open systems and practices will remain relevant well into the future. Forging and Maintaining Open Communities Exploring the Structures that Support Open Improving Access Points for Open Navigating Choice and Engagement in Open Reflecting on Our Past to Build an Open Future “Open Movements” helps practitioners engage more thoughtfully in work that supports not just broad access to information, but also public empowerment. Title Exploring School Librarians’ Perceptions of Digital Books Authors Etienne Vallée, Doctoral Student Department of Educational Technology, Boise State University Jesús Trespalacios, Department of Educational Technology, Boise State University Source School Library Research (SLR) Volume 29, 2026 Abstract Digital books have been available for decades, but many school librarians have been reluctant to expand their digital collection holdings (ebooks and audiobooks) for several reasons. Over the past two decades, research on the acceptance of digital books has mainly focused on universities and college students. This study aims to fill a gap by examining the attitudes and specific challenges faced by school librarians in the rural state of New Hampshire (USA). This exploratory qualitative research study, centered on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), examines school librarians’ attitudes and perceptions toward the ease of use and usefulness of digital books in the school library collection. The findings reveal that while participating school librarians perceive digital books as useful and generally easy to use, technology acceptance remains highly conditional. items.title: Company News: Springer Nature and Google DeepMind Announcing a Research Partnership to Co-Design an AI Peer Review Assistant
items.raw_text: From a Joint Release (Full Text): Peer reviewers play an essential role in safeguarding the quality and integrity of published research. With this in mind, Springer Nature and Google DeepMind are announcing a research partnership to co-design an AI peer review assistant to explore how technology can help create a more rewarding reviewer experience. The assistant will help researchers to review papers more effectively, support them in navigating manuscripts, and identify areas that may need closer attention so they can spend more time on the questions that require specialist scientific judgement. The partnership brings together Springer Nature’s expertise in managing peer review and Google DeepMind’s frontier Gemini models. Building on Google’s experience in developing proven agentic research tools like ScholarPeer and Deep Review , the new assistant helps reviewers analyse large amounts of text, charts, and figures. The prototype assistant currently being tested will help re-envision peer review as an interactive experience that uses AI to empower scientific experts while keeping expert human judgment at the centre of the process. This project is part of Springer Nature’s ongoing commitment to deliver a more frictionless publishing process for authors and peer reviewers which includes its in-house platform, Snapp. Saskia Steinacker, Chief Product Officer, Springer Nature said: “The expertise and judgement of reviewers are fundamental to peer review. items.title: New Report From Tow-Knight Center: “The Three-Layer Cake: Public-Interest Information in an Al-Intermediated Age”; Libraries, Archives, Scholarly Publishers, and Other Groups Mentioned
items.raw_text: From the Tow-Knight Center For Journalism (CUNY): As artificial intelligence reshapes how people find and consume news, a new report from the Tow-Knight Center for Journalism Futures at the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at CUNY examines what it will take to ensure the public has access to reliable, relevant information. The Three-Layer Cake: Public-Interest Information in an AI-Intermediated Age draws on a year of convenings and conversations with journalists, technologists, funders, investors, and other experts. It considers how journalism must evolve as AI systems increasingly stand between information providers and the people they serve. [Clip] The report outlines three connected layers: the products that identify what people want to know, the systems that synthesize answers, and the organizations that produce the underlying reporting. Each layer, the report argues, requires attention and distinct strategies to serve the public interest. The report identifies several priorities for collective action, including shared standards that allow sourcing, context, and other essential information to travel with individual facts as AI systems use them. It also calls for greater visibility into how those systems select information and frame answers. items.title: New Version Available: Principles of Transparency and Best Practice in Scholarly Publishing
items.raw_text: From a Joint Announcement: The Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE), the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), the Open Access Scholarly Publishing Association (OASPA), and the World Association of Medical Editors (WAME) are scholarly organisations that have worked together to identify principles of transparency and best practice for scholarly journals. This is the fifth version of a work in progress (published xxxx 2026). We encourage its wide sharing. The Principles of Transparency and Best Practice in Scholarly Publishing apply to all published journal content, including special issues and conference proceedings. Where practices vary from the standards outlined, editors must clearly state the procedures that the journal follows. COPE, DOAJ, OASPA, and WAME agree that these principles are the foundation of good publishing practice and that publishers must demonstrate that they are being met. Because these principles form the basis of eac organisation’s membership criteria, journals and publishers may need to explain when they do not comply with them. items.title: Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) Libraries Launches Open Index Project to Track the Evolution of Open Knowledge
items.raw_text: From a CMU Libraries Announcement: Carnegie Mellon University Libraries has launched the Open Index Project , a new initiative designed to make the evolution of open knowledge easier to discover and understand. Over the last few decades, open access publishing, open data, open source and other open practices have changed how knowledge moves from discovery to dissemination and reuse. At the same time, the landscape surrounding openness has continued to change. The Open Index Project collects and contextualizes important moments across the field, creating a resource for those interested in understanding how it has developed over time. STEM Librarians Chasz Griego and Huajin Wang led the development of the Open Index Project, with contributions from other members of the Open at CMU team. [Clip] The Open Index Tracker is an interactive dataset that brings together key resources and milestones in open knowledge. Users can filter entries by open area or category to explore resources such as dashboards and landmark reports. Each entry provides a concise summary and context for understanding its significance. [Clip] Building toward the Open Index Report The Tracker and Timeline also provide a foundation for the next phase of the project. This project highlights a strategic partnership between the Community Workshop Series (CWS) at University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, School of Data and Information Sciences (UNC SDIS) and two local public libraries to launch a foundational AI literacy program. The curriculum demystifies AI for adult patrons by fostering familiarity and critical awareness, helping community members navigate these tools effectively and understand their societal impact. To evaluate the program in Spring 2026, a post-workshop survey measured shifts in participant confidence and self-efficacy. The survey utilizes a 5-point Likert scale to compare confidence levels regarding AI before and after the class, while also measuring participants’ grasp of ethical complexities and the accessibility of instructional support. items.title: Erica Kent On The Light And Shadows Of Her Magnificent New Novel
items.raw_text: Reader’s first meet Jessica Ryder, the captivating protagonist of Erica Kent’s Black Dog , as a smart and brash eleven-year-old living with her alcoholic father in Brookline, Massachusetts. It’s 1980 and Jessica, an ardent music fan, is devastated over the death of John Lennon. In a misguided attempt to comfort her, Jessica’s father offers her a beer. This fateful act kicks off a near-decade long struggle with alcohol and drugs, which Kent depicts with clarity and empathy. Kent masterfully charts Jessica’s adolescence as the young woman negotiates her complicated family dynamic, not only with her father, but also with her mother and sister, who live in a far different socioeconomic world in nearby Boston. What follows is not only a riveting coming of age story but also a clear-eyed examination of the often fraught road to recovery. The reviews have been rapturous for Black Dog . Library Journal wrote, “Kent demonstrates her skills with evocative and atmospheric prose” and Pulitzer-Prize winner Richard Russo raved, “Erica Kent’s Black Dog takes the reader on a truly terrifying journey, but guess what? I’m so, so glad I fastened my seatbelt, gritted my teeth, and climbed aboard.” Kent spoke with us about using her setting as a character, capturing Jessica’s voice, and allowing the story to find her. When Ash was a baby, her mother died a fiery death soon after police discovered she was The Clossdale Killer, a serial killer whose victims were all popular high school girls. Years later, when five of Ash’s classmates disappear and townspeople discover dead bodies in the forest, all signs point to Ash as the most logical suspect. Over the course of one terrifying night, Ash teams up with her only two friends, Cassie and Jamie, to discover the real culprit, guided by their mantra WWJLCD (What Would Jamie Lee Curtis Do?). Laugh out loud funny with surprising twists, Beck Kubrick’s Dead Girls is a taut thriller that deftly upends the slasher genre. Critics have praised the graphic novel, with Kirkus Reviews hailing it as a “chilling slasher that effectively explores legacy, identity, confronting the past—and refusing to be defined by it.” We spoke to Kubrick about constructing the elaborate mysteries Dead Girls , playing with the framework of horror, and the “terrible feral” high schoolers at the heart of the story. Dead Girls is so exciting and unnerving. I was curious to hear you talk about what was fun about exploring the world of a slasher film in a graphic novel. items.title: E-Rate Under Threat: Take a Stand and Show Up for E-Rate
items.raw_text: After thirty years of keeping libraries online, the E-Rate program has seen its share of challenges. Just in the last two years, the program weathered the loss of support for hotspot lending and suffered through a Supreme Court Challenge . While the Supreme Court decision ultimately went in our favor, there is no time to sit back and relax for library advocates. In June, the Federal Communication’s Commission (FCC) launched a proceeding (officially, a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking) that threatens to terminate this vital program. Now is the time to show up for E-Rate and tell the FCC what broadband access at your library means for your community. A Quick E-Rate Refresher One of four programs within the FCC’s Universal Service Fund, set up in the 1996 Telecommunications Act, the E-Rate program was established to ensure public libraries and K-12 schools have affordable access to advanced telecommunications (i.e., broadband and internet access). Today, E-Rate provides funding to almost three-quarters of public libraries to help offset monthly internet service costs and the costs for eligible technology necessary for making sure Wi-Fi is available throughout the building. How much are we talking about? Currently the program sends about $2.4 billion to public libraries and K-12 schools annually. items.title: Bringing Big Ideas Home: Reflections from PLA 2026 in Minneapolis
items.raw_text: The most valuable takeaway from my time at the Public Library Association Conference wasn’t just new ideas; it was a renewed sense of purpose. As the director of a small, rural library in Elba, Alabama, I was thrilled to receive a PLA scholarship to attend the conference in Minneapolis. PLA has supported our library in meaningful ways over the years, including a 2019 grant that funded a high school intern. That student is now about to graduate from college and, inspired by her experience at our library, is pursuing her MLS. Moments like that are a powerful reminder of the long-term impact of library work. Energy, Inspiration, and Hard Conversations I attended with a colleague from a neighboring library, and from the moment we walked into the Minneapolis Convention Center, the energy was contagious. We immediately felt welcomed, not just by the upbeat registration staff but by the shared sense of purpose among attendees. The opening session set the tone. Hearing from speakers, including Bryan Stevenson, was both inspiring and challenging. His remarks encouraged me to reflect more deeply on local history in my own community, including the possibility of researching and acknowledging difficult chapters like lynchings. I left with a desire to partner with our local historical preservation group to explore ways to honor and remember those stories. items.title: Building Acceptance and Community at PLA 2026
items.raw_text: My name is Lana Sweeting, and I was lucky enough to be selected for a 2026 PLA scholarship. I serve as an Adult Reference Librarian in Portland, Oregon, where much of my work focuses on serving the Black community through programming, collections, and outreach. While there were many sessions that were relevant and helpful to my everyday work, two in particular invigorated my work as a public librarian. First, I felt very drawn to the session “Every Story Matters, Every Body Belongs: Fat Inclusive Libraries.” The presenter, Amelia Mason, was absolutely wonderful and very knowledgeable on the subject. I was locked in from the very first slide, which simply said, “I Am Fat.” The honest and positive energy went up from there. Along with sharing quantitative data, Amelia discussed myths surrounding fatness, as well as history, race, fat acceptance and neutrality, and how these issues apply to library spaces and other spaces we regularly occupy. For example, Amelia noted that PLA shirts on the website only went up to size 3XL. After the session, I felt informed and inspired to take this information back to Multnomah County Library. The session included a resource booklist that inspired me to create a booklist and display for my own library and begin conversations around diversity audits of our catalog so we can make relevant materials more accessible. items.title: The Future Is Now: Black Men in Libraries
items.raw_text: I appreciated the chance to attend the PLA 2026 Conference. As an early-career librarian and MLIS student at the University of South Florida, I had no idea what to expect, but I am proud to report that I was not let down. I came to Minneapolis with a strong desire to learn more about public libraries, and I did just that. I learned more about how to strengthen library boards and foundations, how to protect queer and trans staff, and how to provide library services to those who are incarcerated. I am really happy with my experience. I attended various community-related sessions because it is so important to build relationships and have a sense of belonging, especially in today’s tumultuous political climate. This is also important in my Master of Library and Information Science (MLIS) journey, where I promote positive connections, encourage librarians to embrace diversity, and build relationships with those around them. PLA was an amazing conference filled with experts who were welcoming and eager to answer questions from the audience. It was difficult to choose just one program to highlight because I genuinely enjoyed all the sessions. However, one stood out to me. My favorite was Black Men in Libraries: Our History, Our Heroes, and Our Horizon . items.title: ALA Launches Reporting Form for Incidents Against Immigrants in Libraries
items.raw_text: Acknowledgments: The author thanks Hayley Park of the University of Maryland for her contributions to language used in this article and Derek Wilmott of the University of Toledo for his assistance in developing the incident reporting form. Libraries across the country are navigating heightened immigration enforcement activity while trying to support community members and staff. Library leaders may face difficult decisions about how to respond to enforcement activity, address harassment, communicate with their communities, and protect patrons and employees, often with limited information about what other libraries are experiencing. Consider a public library responding to increased immigration enforcement activity in its community. Library leadership might consider issuing a public statement supporting immigrants but ultimately decide against it after consulting legal counsel, concerned that doing so could make the library a target. How can library leaders make decisions like this when much of the information available to them comes from anecdotal experiences or informal conversations with colleagues? Better data can help. items.title: Art for Everyone: How Public Libraries Expand Access
items.raw_text: Introducing children to viewing, creating, and enjoying art at a young age helps them appreciate it throughout their lives. Some children are exposed to various forms of art because it is part of their daily life or because they have easy access to museums and galleries in their community. But in many areas across the country, access to museums and art galleries can be cost prohibitive. That is where the public library comes in! While some museums, including the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., offer free admission, millions of people across the country do not have easy access to them. According to the 2024 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers from the American Alliance of Museums and Wilkening Consulting, museum admission costs vary widely, from a few dollars to $40–$50 per adult at some institutions. Among U.S. adults who visit museums at least occasionally, cost was the number one barrier to visiting more often. Among frequent museum-goers, younger adults were twice as likely as seniors to be concerned about admission costs. In response to those barriers, and in an effort to enrich and inspire customers of all ages, many library systems have stepped up to provide access to art in a variety of forms. When Taryn lands a chance to audition for Starmaker , the television show that has become a global phenomenon and launched past winners to superstardom, it seems like the best opportunity for her to provide her brother with desperately needed medical care. Yet when she begins rehearsing with her fellow contestants, Taryn must confront the challenge of collaborating and competing with contestants whose success could mean her death. items.title: Autism Acceptance at All Ages
items.raw_text: Autism acceptance efforts have come a long way in recent years, and libraries are one of the key reasons why. As a librarian and the mother of two sons with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), I’ve witnessed this progress firsthand. In my capacity as the assistant director of the Beals Memorial Library (BML), I’ve seen how efforts to create more inclusive programs, services, and spaces can promote positive social change that dra-matically improves people’s quality of life, disabled or not. Through our “See Beyond the Spectrum” initiative, in recent years, BML has established new ASD-friendly programs, made our existing programs more accessible, updated our collections with texts by autistic writers, and established an autism caregiver support group. Our staff have gone through autism awareness training, and we’ve established partnerships with local organizations that serve autistic youth. Much of this workhas been supported by external grants, including generous funding from the ALA’s “Libraries Transforming Communities” initiative, which seeks to help libraries become more accessible to patrons with disabilities. Everything we’ve done has proved beneficial, both inside and outside of the library. Staff-patron interactions are more productive and less awkward. Families feel welcomed, and patrons with ASD feel comfortable being themselves when they visit. Community members are more knowledgeable about ASD and are actively talking about it. items.title: The Librarian’s New Role: Knowledge Discovery
items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. It represents a fundamental change in the relationship between people and information. The question librarians should be asking is not whether artificial intelligence can answer questions. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.title: Making the Invisible Visible: Advocacy at the Heart of Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Public libraries face no shortage of challenges today. Ongoing censorship efforts, increasing threats to staff safety, growing public distrust of institutions, and rapid technological change continue to reshape the work of libraries and the people who sustain them. In this environment, advocacy matters more than ever. That message came through clearly at the 2026 Public Library Association conference, where many sessions focused on helping librarians strengthen their advocacy skills. At the heart of every library are the workers who understand its value best and are often its strongest advocates. One session I attended, “Advocacy at the Core of ALA’s Next 150 Years,” featured Sam Helmick, Maria McCauley, Daniel Montgomery, and Lisa Varga. The panel offered practical strategies for advocacy, including using easy digital tools to contact legislators, participating in National Library Legislative Day, supporting legislation such as the Right to Read Act, and inviting elected officials into library spaces to see the work firsthand. Another standout session, “Advocacy Strategies for Getting Things Done,” featured Lisa Wells, Amanda Kordeliski, Tim Miller, Gail Oehler, and Kelly Sitzman from libraries across Oklahoma. Their discussion focused on the power of quiet advocacy. Quiet advocacy means building relationships with legislators before you urgently need their support. items.title: Creating Meaningful Connections Through Memory Cafés
items.raw_text: The 2026 Public Library Association conference featured many excellent sessions focused on programming and community engagement, but one that especially resonated with me was “Memory Cafés in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections,” presented by Christina M. Johnson, Allan M. Kleiman, and Susan H. McFadden. Before attending this session, I had heard of Memory Cafés but did not fully understand what they were, who they served, or how they could be integrated into library programming. By the end of the hour, I felt equipped with the knowledge and resources needed to successfully bring this type of program to my own library. The library where I work is within walking distance of two senior living apartment buildings, and our community of 16,000 is also home to several assisted living facilities. Older adults often make up the majority of attendees at our programs, so as the staff member responsible for adult programming, I attended PLA hoping to learn about meaningful services for this audience. The session began by defining the core audience for a Memory Café: people living with dementia, whether formally diagnosed or not, their caregivers, and volunteers interested in learning more. items.title: From Skeptic to Troublemaker: One Book Club Idea That Changed My Mind
items.raw_text: I’ll admit it: library book clubs make me instantly wary. People constantly ask libraries to offer them, only to never actually show up. And a book club for kids? Forget about it. They already have plenty of assigned reading at school. So when I attended Tanvi Rastogi’s session, “Speak Up: Using Middle Grade Books to Build Allyship Muscles,” I assumed it would be a low-stakes hour to slowly wake up and drink my coffee. Friends, I didn’t even need the coffee. I left energized. Rastogi’s book club model, Good Books Young Troublemakers (GBYT), is far more than a well-intentioned idea with a catchy title. It has its own website and 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status, a sign of just how thoroughly Rastogi developed this concept after first dreaming it up in the shower. She has created a turnkey model for anyone interested in starting a chapter. Each month features a thoughtfully selected recently published title, paired with a robust downloadable discussion guide. New chapter leaders can request a starter kit complete with stickers and bookmarks mailed directly to them. Best of all, it’s free, though donations are encouraged, and there’s a pretty fun sticker if you decide to support the work. So what is GBYT all about? items.title: “I Wanted To Write Something That Felt More Like A Hug” – DeAndra Davis On Her Enchanting Coming-Of-Age Novel
items.raw_text: Despite being smart, funny, and her class’s valedictorian, Jaliya has spent much of her high school career ignored by her classmates. After graduation, her dad encourages her to leave their South Florida home to spend the summer in Jamaica with her family, who she hasn’t seen in several years. Although reluctant to do so, Jaliya changes her mind after receiving an unsigned letter postmarked from Jamaica asking when she’s going to return there. Convinced the letter is from her estranged mother, Jaliya devises a plan to return to Jamaica, find her mother, and figure out once and for all why she left their family long ago. Yet once she’s back in Jamaica, Jaliya’s life grows unexpectedly richer. She reconnects with childhood friends and finds herself caught in a love triangle between her schoolgirl crush, Andre, and an intriguing new girl, India, who has just moved to her cousin’s neighborhood. items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials.
